title: Scaffolds for Dominating the Article of the Week
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart follows up his history with Kelly Gallagher's article of the week by publishing the scaffolds he built around it - rubrics, Reading for Meaning statements from Perini, Silver and Dewing, They Say/I Say frames and a self-editing checklist - but the two warnings he puts in front of the resources are what carry the piece. The first is to stay clear about purpose, and he lets Gallagher answer it himself from the previous post's comments: the single goal is that kids get smarter about the world, and time pressure is precisely why Gallagher never built rubrics or took the assignment deeper. The second is Jerry Graff's 'courseocentrism,' the tunnel vision in which a teacher's own course becomes the whole world and nobody takes an interest in what colleagues are teaching. Stuart turns that critique on the article of the week itself: a good practice can metastasize and crowd out the curriculum a district actually mandated. He backs it with Marzano on the power of a guaranteed and viable curriculum, then adds that it is also simply about making school sensible for kids. His ceiling is concrete - about fifteen minutes Monday and fifteen Friday, roughly ten percent of weekly instructional time - and the scaffolds themselves are offered as-needed rather than as a standing weekly packet.
points: The governing discipline is purpose-first, and Gallagher's own comment supplies it: one goal, that kids get smarter about the world, which is why he never built rubrics for the assignment.
Stuart imports Graff's 'courseocentrism' into K-12 to argue that a teacher's favorite practice can quietly displace the curriculum that colleagues and the district are counting on.
He converts 'don't overdo it' into a budget a teacher can check - roughly 15 minutes Monday and 15 Friday, about 10 percent of weekly instructional time, significant but not curriculum-dominating.
The scaffolds are explicitly as-needed rather than a standing weekly packet, so support fades as students grow instead of hardening into a routine.

He grounds the anti-courseocentrism point in Marzano's finding that a guaranteed, viable curriculum is a powerful school-level factor in achievement, then adds the simpler reason: it makes school sensible for kids.
quotes: I have one simple goal for the AoW assignment—that my kids get smarter about the world. Because of time limitations—and because of all the other things I have to teach—I have not created rubrics or taken the AoW deeper.

At the end of the day, my job as a freshman world history and English teacher is to provide students with a quality course of study in what my district lays out as the English 9 and the world history curricula. I need to work with my colleagues in those courses to avoid what Jerry Graff calls “courseocentrism.

It's my privilege and pleasure to wrestle with how to help them do that in the most productive, authentic, long-term-flourishing-promoting ways possible. My English 9 kids do need to read the texts Cedar Springs Public Schools have mandated for English 9.

Even though Graff is writing about postsecondary settings, I have seen this phenomenon clearly enough in every setting and grade level I've taught. Marzano's research says this is bad — having a quality, guaranteed, viable curriculum is a powerful school-related factor in raising student achievement. But it's not just about Marzano's research — it's also about making school more sensible for kids.

Yes, dear reader, we are. I'm simply saying this: resist the temptation to allow article of the week to take over huge swaths of your courses; resist the temptation to let students do the whole thing in class, every single week, if your curriculum doesn't call for it.

If you'd like a percentage of instructional time to aim for, my goal is to spend ~15 minutes on Mondays and ~15 minutes on Fridays for article of the week, and that's 10 percent of my weekly instructional time with world history students. 10 percent is significant but not curriculum-dominating.

I think Mr. Gallagher would agree with me that the last thing AoW should become is a curriculum nuking time-filler. My world history kids do need to learn and grapple with world history content. It's my privilege and pleasure to wrestle with how to help them do that in the most productive, authentic, long-term-flourishing-promoting ways possible.
